mainEntity.name: How long does a bad taste last after a filling?

acceptedAnswer.text: In most cases, a mild or unusual taste following a filling resolves within 24 to 72 hours. Composite fillings may leave a slight chemical or bitter taste initially as the bonding agents fully set, whilst amalgam fillings can produce a more pronounced metallic sensation. If the taste persists beyond three to five days, or if it worsens or is accompanied by pain or sensitivity, it is a good idea to contact your dental practice for a review.

mainEntity.name: Is a metallic taste after dental work something to worry about?

acceptedAnswer.text: A metallic taste after dental treatment is very common and is typically nothing to worry about. It can result from minor bleeding during the procedure, exposure to metals in restorative materials, or trace components of local anaesthetic. This sensation is usually short-lived. However, if the metallic taste persists over several days without improvement, a dental review is a reasonable and sensible step.

mainEntity.name: Why does my filling taste like chemicals?

acceptedAnswer.text: A chemical taste after a composite filling is usually caused by trace amounts of the bonding agent or uncured resin monomer present in the early hours after placement. Once the filling has fully set and saliva has had time to neutralise the area, this taste should fade. If you notice the taste returning or worsening days after treatment, it could be worth asking your dentist to check the restoration.

mainEntity.name: Can a bad taste after a filling mean there is an infection?

acceptedAnswer.text: A bad taste alone following a routine filling is not necessarily a sign of infection. However, if the taste is notably foul or fetid, and is accompanied by swelling, throbbing pain, fever, or a sense of pressure in the jaw, these signs together may indicate a developing dental infection and should be assessed professionally without delay. Early evaluation helps to ensure appropriate management and a comfortable recovery.

mainEntity.name: What is dry socket and does it cause a bad taste?

acceptedAnswer.text: Dry socket (alveolar osteitis) occurs when the blood clot that forms in a tooth extraction socket is dislodged or fails to develop properly, leaving the underlying bone exposed. It typically produces a distinctive unpleasant taste and odour, alongside a dull aching pain that may radiate toward the ear. Dry socket usually develops two to four days after extraction. It is a recognised post-extraction complication and is managed by your dental practice, so do contact them if you suspect you may be experiencing it.

mainEntity.name: Is it normal to have a bad taste after a root canal?

acceptedAnswer.text: A mild unusual taste following root canal treatment is not uncommon and may be related to the irrigants and medicaments used during the procedure, or the temporary dressing placed in the tooth. This generally resolves within a few days. If the taste is persistently unpleasant, or if you develop pain or swelling in the days following treatment, contacting your dentist for a review is entirely appropriate.
